hook.support: A course ad says: “Sign up today and get a free laptop!” Sounds good. But what is the course? What does it cost? Is it real? Before you sign up, check.
hook.core: An ad pops up: “Get your diploma online. Free laptop when you enrol today!” Sounds like a great deal. But what’s the course, who runs it, what does it really cost, and is the information even true? Thousands of Australians learned the hard way to check first.
hook.extend: Choosing a course or apprenticeship is a big decision: months or years of your time, and sometimes thousands of dollars of debt. Course information comes from many places, and not all of it is accurate, current or honest. Checking it like a researcher protects your time and your money.

why.support: A course can take years and cost a lot. Checking first saves you from a bad deal.
why.core: TAFE courses and apprenticeships can shape the next few years of your life. Checking the facts first means you pick the right course, at the right price, with a real provider.
why.extend: Choosing training is a high-stakes decision. Being able to locate sources and judge their accuracy and validity protects you from poor choices and predatory providers, and it’s a research skill you’ll use in any course you take.

articles.title: Check before you sign up

body.support:
Thinking about a TAFE course or an apprenticeship? Check the facts first.

**Find the key facts:**
- What is the course called?
- How long does it take?
- What does it cost?
- What do you need to start?
- When does it start?
- Who runs it?
.
**Where to look:**
- the TAFE’s own course page.
- the **Victorian Skills Gateway**, a government site for courses.
- **Free TAFE**: some courses cost nothing for tuition, if you’re eligible. You may still pay for materials.
.
**Then check it.** Ask four questions.
1. **Who says?** Is it the official page, or an ad?
2. **When?** Is it this year’s information?
3. **Does it match?** Do two sources say the same thing?
4. **What’s the catch?** Free gifts and pressure to sign today are warning signs.
body.core:
Thinking about a TAFE course or an apprenticeship? It could shape the next few years of your life, so check the facts before you sign anything.

**Find the key facts.** Course name, length, cost, entry requirements, start dates, where and how it runs (on campus, online, at work), and who the **provider** is.

**Find good sources.**
- the provider’s own course page.
- the **Victorian Skills Gateway**, the Victorian Government’s course search.
- **training.gov.au**, the national list of real qualifications and **registered** training providers.
- the Victorian Government’s **Free TAFE** list. Tuition is free for many courses if you’re eligible (for example, an Australian citizen or permanent resident), but you may still pay materials fees.

**Then check what you found.** Ask four questions.
1. **Who says?** The official provider or government, or someone selling something? An ad’s job is to persuade you.
2. **When?** Is it **current**? Look for this year’s dates and fees. Old pages can be wrong.
3. **Does it match?** Compare two sources. If the length or cost is different, find out which is right. Call or email the provider and ask.
4. **What’s the catch?** Free laptops, gifts, “sign up today” pressure, or a course that seems too easy are warning signs. So is any course that leaves you with a big debt you don’t understand.
body.extend:
Choosing a TAFE course or apprenticeship is a significant decision, so treat it like research: locate good sources, then test the information for **accuracy** (is it correct?) and **validity** (is it sound and trustworthy?).

**Key facts to establish:** course title and national code, length, cost, entry requirements, start dates, delivery mode (campus, online, workplace), and the **provider**.

**Sources, from most to least authoritative:**
- **training.gov.au**: the national register of qualifications and **registered** training organisations (RTOs). If a provider or course isn’t listed, the qualification may not be recognised.
- the **Victorian Skills Gateway**: the state government’s course search.
- the provider’s own course page.
- the **Free TAFE** list: tuition is free for eligible students (such as Australian citizens and permanent residents) in listed courses, though materials fees may still apply.
- reviews, forums and social media: useful for experiences, unreliable for facts.

**Testing the information:**
1. **Authority.** Who published it, and what do they gain? Marketing is designed to persuade.
2. **Currency.** Are dates and fees for this intake? Outdated pages are a common source of error.
3. **Corroboration.** Do two independent sources agree on the code, length and cost? If not, contact the provider and resolve the difference.
4. **Red flags.** Inducements such as free devices, pressure to enrol immediately, unrealistic promises, or unclear debt are warning signs. Misleading sales tactics in vocational education have resulted in some of Australia’s largest consumer-law penalties.

caseStudies.title: The free laptop that cost thousands

body.support:
In the 2010s, the government lent people money for some courses. They paid it back later, through tax.

A training college called **Phoenix Institute** signed up lots of people. Its courses cost **$18,000 to $21,000** each. Some people were offered free gifts, like a laptop.

Many didn’t know they were taking on a big debt.

In **2023**, a court ordered Phoenix and its sales company to pay **$438 million** in penalties. That was a record. The court found they misled students.
body.core:
In the 2010s, the government had a loan scheme called **VET FEE-HELP**. Students could do some courses now and pay the cost back later, through the tax system.

A training college called **Phoenix Institute**, and its sales company, signed up many students to online diploma courses costing **$18,000 to $21,000** each. Sales agents offered incentives, like a free device. Many people didn’t understand they were taking on a large debt.

Phoenix received more than **$106 million** from the government.

In **2023**, the Federal Court ordered Phoenix and its sales company to pay **$438 million** in penalties, a record for this kind of case. The court found they had misled students and acted unconscionably, which means extremely unfairly. Students who didn’t finish had their debts cancelled.
body.extend:
In the mid-2010s, a loan scheme called VET FEE-HELP let students enrol in job-training courses and pay the cost back later, through the tax system. Some private colleges took advantage of it.

**Phoenix Institute of Australia** and its sales company, Community Training Initiatives, enrolled many people in online diploma courses. Each cost **$18,000 to $21,000**. Recruiters used offers such as free devices. Many people didn’t understand they were taking on a large debt. Phoenix received more than **$106 million** from the federal government.

In July **2023**, the Federal Court ordered the two companies to pay record penalties of **$438 million**. The court found they had misled students and treated them extremely unfairly. The debts of students who didn’t finish were cancelled. By then, VET FEE-HELP had been replaced by a stricter scheme.

The case shows why the source of course information matters. The people selling these courses earned money from each enrolment, whether or not the course suited the student.

**Course:** Certificate II in Animal Care, at our local TAFE.

**Sources:** the TAFE’s course page, and the Victorian Skills Gateway.

**What matches:** both say about 6 months, part-time, starting in February. Both say it’s Free TAFE.

**What doesn’t match:** the TAFE page says there’s a $180 materials fee. The Gateway doesn’t mention it. The TAFE page was updated this month, so I trust it more. I’ll ask at the open day.

**Catch?** No gifts, no pressure.

**My decision:** Yes. I want to work at a vet clinic, and it fits around my job.

teacher.answers:
**Sort:** TAFE page this year — trust; Facebook comment — check; free laptop ad — check; training.gov.au — trust; updated 2019 — check; Skills Gateway — trust.

**Annotation:** 1 course name and code (check on training.gov.au); 2 provider (registered?); 3 length and mode; 4 entry requirements; 5 cost (free tuition, but materials fee); 6 start dates and currency.

**Case study:** incentives like free devices and signing people up quickly; many didn’t understand the VET FEE-HELP debt; “Who says?” and “What’s the catch?” would have helped most.

realityCheck: **Some students have no idea what they want to study.** Let them check a course a friend, sibling or parent is considering, or one linked to a job they’d like.
**Course websites are long and full of jargon.** Model scanning for the six key facts; don’t expect students to read whole pages.
**Free TAFE eligibility is personal.** Don’t ask students about their residency or visa status in class.
**The case study can feel abstract.** It lands when you show the original kind of ad (“free laptop!”) and ask who it was aimed at.
**Works in a real class:** yes, especially with an open day or a TAFE visit soon after.
